successors.name: British Colonial Empire
successors.text: Canada with all its dependencies (the Saint Lawrence valley, the Great Lakes and Ohio posts, Acadia's remnant, Ile Royale)

successors.name: Spanish Louisiana
successors.text: Louisiana west of the Mississippi with New Orleans

successors.name: Kingdom of France
successors.text: France recovered the two small islands from Britain and kept fishing rights off Newfoundland (Treaty of Paris page)

capitals.name: Saint Croix Island, then Port-Royal (Annapolis Royal)

ledger.x: 1604: the French settle Saint Croix Island, the first colony of New France.
1608: Champlain founds Quebec.
1608: the seat of New France moves from Acadia to Quebec, the capital the infobox gives.
1627: New France passes to the Company of One Hundred Associates.
1629: the English also hold Acadia and Cape Breton Island.
1629 (19 July): Quebec surrenders to the English.
1632 (29 March): the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye gives New France back.
1642: the Saint Lawrence settlement runs up to Montreal.
1654: the English take Acadia again.
1659: Cape Breton Island falls empty.
1662: Plaisance on Newfoundland's Placentia Bay.
1663: New France becomes a royal province.
1668: the Sault Sainte Marie mission, the first French post on the upper Great Lakes.
1670: Acadia returns to France.
1671: the Michilimackinac mission.
1673: Fort Frontenac on Lake Ontario.
1673: Cliopatria draws four cells at Green Bay.
1677: the Saint Lawrence shape grows from 93 to 120 cells; no page opened dates it.
1678: Fort Niagara.
1682: Fort Saint Louis on the Illinois River, the Illinois Country's first lasting post.
1683: the Saint Lawrence shape grows again; no page opened dates it.
1686: Arkansas Post.
1686 (March): New France strikes the English posts on James Bay.
1686 (March): the James Bay posts are taken.
1687: three cells on the Texas coast and a Wisconsin dot appear in Cliopatria's shape; none of the pages opened mentions them.
1691: the Texas cells leave Cliopatria's shape.
1696: Cahokia.
1697 (5 September): d'Iberville's second raid on York Factory.
1699: Old Biloxi.
1701: Detroit.
1702 (January): Mobile.
1710: the British take Port-Royal.
1713: Cape Breton, as Ile Royale, is French again and Louisbourg is founded.
1713 (April): the occupation of peninsular Nova Scotia ends in cession.
1713 (11 April): Utrecht cedes Nova Scotia.
1713 (11 April): Utrecht cedes France's claims to Newfoundland.
1713 (April): the Hudson Bay contest ends.
1713 (April): the Hudson Bay posts go to Britain.
1714: Natchitoches.
1716: Fort Rosalie at Natchez.
1718: New Orleans.
1718: Cliopatria adds a dot in Alabama (32.8 N 86.6 W) and a cluster at 41.1 N 86.3 W on the Michigan-Indiana line; none of the pages opened mentions them.
1721: Ile Saint-Jean (Prince Edward Island) joins Cliopatria's shape.

1721: the Louisiana shape thickens from 75 to 170 cells along the Mississippi and the Gulf coast; the Louisiana page dates posts, not this growth (Crozat 1712 to 1731 and the Company years are undated on it).
1727: Fort Beauharnois on the upper Mississippi.
1731: Fort Saint-Pierre on Rainy Lake.
1732: Fort Saint-Charles on Lake of the Woods, La Vérendrye's headquarters.
1734: Fort Maurepas on Lake Winnipeg.
1734: Cliopatria's big cluster grows from 147 to 322 cells, filling the ground between Canada, New Brunswick and Maine.
1738 (October): Fort La Reine.
1741: Cliopatria adds 13 cells in Manitoba (Lake Winnipeg to 101 W).
1753: Fort Presque Isle and Fort Le Boeuf, then Fort Duquesne in 1754, carry New France into the Ohio Country.
1754 (April): the Ohio Country is fought for.
1755 (June): Fort Beauséjour falls.
1758 (26 July): Louisbourg falls to the British.
1759 (September): Quebec falls.
1760 (8 September): Montreal capitulates and Canada passes under British military occupation.

1760 (8 September): the Ohio fighting ends with the capitulation of Montreal; the page records Fort Duquesne's fall in neither month nor year (it dates only 'the Forbes Expedition... in September-October 1758').
1762 (November): France cedes Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain.
1763 (10 February): the British occupation of Ile Royale ends in cession.
1763 (10 February): the occupation of Quebec ends in cession.
1763 (10 February): the occupation of the rest of Canada ends in cession.
1763 (10 February): France cedes Canada.
1763 (10 February): France cedes Cape Breton and the islands of the Gulf.
1763 (10 February): Louisiana east of the Mississippi goes to Britain.
1763: New France ends.

wars.name: Anglo-French War (1627-1629)
wars.outcome: English victory on the ground: David Kirke's fleet forced Quebec to surrender on 19 July 1629 after the treaty of Susa; the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye of 29 March 1632 returned Quebec, Acadia and Cape Breton Island.

wars.name: King William's War
wars.outcome: No border change: 'At the end of the war in 1697, England returned the territory to France in the Treaty of Ryswick'; Acadia had been 'notionally integrated into the newly formed Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691'.

wars.name: Hudson Bay conflict (1686-1713)
wars.outcome: French raids took the James Bay posts in 1686 and York Factory in 1694 (recovered by the company in 1695) and 1697; 'The French retained all of the outposts except Fort Albany until 1713', when Utrecht made France 'relinquish all claims to Great Britain on…

wars.name: Queen Anne's War
wars.outcome: British victory: Acadia 'was conquered in 1710 during Queen Anne's War' and Utrecht (11 April 1713) ceded Nova Scotia, the Newfoundland claims and the Hudson Bay territories, while France kept Cape Breton Island.

wars.name: French and Indian War
wars.outcome: British victory: Fort Beauséjour (June 1755), Louisbourg (26 July 1758 per the Ile-Royale page), Quebec (September 1759) and Montreal (8 September 1760) fell; the Treaty of Paris of 10 February 1763 ceded Canada, Cape Breton and Louisiana east of the…

certainty.note: Settlements, forts and claims, not surveyed lines: the Pays d'en Haut and Ohio posts are points in Indigenous land, the Kennebec River claim was contested, and the Utrecht page names no boundary commission for Acadia or Hudson Bay.
The Treaty of Paris fixed the Mississippi line 'along the middle of the River Mississippi, from its source to the river Iberville' and then Lakes Maurepas and Pontchartrain to the sea.

sources.title: Pierre Gaultier de Varennes, sieur de La Vérendrye
